conclusion.next_question: Which trade-off does the programme want to own: the simplicity of one model, or the smaller blast radius of several?
paragraphs: Phase 3 set out to establish whether the three candidate architectures differ enough in size, speed, operability and cost for the choice to be made on technical grounds. On the evidence assembled, they do not. All three fit comfortably within ordinary infrastructure under the assumptions tested, and the illustrative costs sit close together.

What does separate them is operational: how much has to be re-tested when one part changes, how far a failure spreads, and how much content would be duplicated across models. Those are the terms in which the decision should be argued.
The largest single influence on model size is not the architecture at all. It is how many other variables each variable depends on, and that is a clinical modelling decision that has not been taken.
conclusion.status_note: The draft ADR remains open. The candidate families are a provisional analytical baseline, and the federated figures will change once clinical review settles the family boundaries.

cost.caveat: These are illustrative scenarios, not a quotation. They are modelled on us-east-1 pricing as a stand-in for eu-west-2, and they price compute for inference only. Treat the gap between the patterns as the finding, not the absolute figures.
cost.floor_note: Below roughly 5,000,000 assessments a month, the patterns cost the same because a minimum amount of capacity has to run regardless of how much work reaches it. The differences only appear once volume is high enough to need more than that minimum.

method_notes.statement: Monthly assessment volumes and peak multiplier are scenarios, not measured 111/999 production traffic.

ALB, observability and artefact storage use explicit monthly allowances. NAT/data transfer, WAF, KMS, ECR, backup and organisational shared-service charges are not yet itemised.

does_not_tell_us: Which architecture should be built. The draft ADR records open decision gates, not a recommendation.
What the system would actually cost. The cost figures are illustrative scenarios built on stated assumptions and non-target-region pricing, not a quotation.
How fast the real system would respond — its production latency. The benchmark runs models a fraction of the size of the real ones; it bounds the shape of the problem, not the answer.
Whether the candidate families are the right ones. They remain a provisional analytical baseline pending clinical review, and every federated figure inherits that caveat.

What the clinically correct Bayesian structure is. The parent counts are a sensitivity range, not a proposed model; a real network would be designed clinically, not derived from the current question ordering.

executive_summary.bottom_line: Phase 3 has assembled the comparison evidence but does not close the decision: 2 gate(s) remain open, and the candidate families are still a provisional baseline awaiting clinical review.
executive_summary.headline: All three architectures are technically feasible at this scale. The decision is not about whether they fit, but about which trade-off is acceptable.
key_points: Representing the content literally needs about 47,983 variables; treating each distinct question once needs 3,787, roughly 13 times fewer.
Splitting into the candidate families needs about 6,990 variable copies, because a question used by several families is held in each of them.
Probability-table size is driven far more by how many other variables each one depends on than by how many variables there are. That structural choice is clinical, and has not been made.
Measured inference timings are in the low milliseconds, but on models a fraction of real size, so they bound the shape of the problem rather than predicting production performance.

Illustrative running costs are identical across the deployment patterns until volume is high enough to need more than minimum capacity; at 5,000,000 assessments a month they spread to about 2.0x between cheapest and dearest, though the absolute sums remain small.

methodology.definition: One thing the model reasons about, usually corresponding to a question and its possible answers. The three representations differ only in what they treat as the same variable.

For each variable, one number for every combination of its own answers and the answers of the variables it depends on. Size is the product of those, not the sum, which is why dependency count dominates.
The numbers that would actually have to be estimated. Each column of a probability table must sum to one, so one value per column follows from the others and is not independently estimated.

How many other variables a variable depends on. Varied deliberately across a range here because the real structure would be a clinical design decision, not something derivable from the current content.
The share of a real model's variables that the benchmarked model actually contained. Coverage well below 100% means the timings describe the trend, not the destination.
A deployment shape: how many services, which models are held in memory, and how requests are routed between them. Deliberately separate from the logical question of how the model is divided.
How much of the system has to be re-tested and re-released when one part changes. A primary operational difference between the patterns.
A scenario built from stated assumptions about volume, compute and pricing. Useful for comparing patterns against each other; not a budget figure and not a quotation.
Current Phase 2 analytical candidate set. Limitation: Pending clinician-led refinement.
Pathway/order Tx occurrence. Limitation: Upper-bound representation, not a clinical BN design.
Distinct QuestionID. Limitation: Does not merge clinically equivalent different QuestionIDs.
Catalogue answer count. Limitation: A future clinical BN may encode states differently.
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. Limitation: Sensitivity only until a BN DAG transformation is agreed.
3203. Limitation: Counts variable copies, not memory or runtime coordination cost.

tells_us.text: Treating each distinct question once rather than once per pathway takes the variable count from 47,983 to 3,787. No other choice in this analysis changes the size by as much.
tells_us.title: Deduplication is the single largest lever on size

tells_us.text: The candidate families need 6,990 variable copies against 3,787 for a single deduplicated model. The difference is the questions used by more than one family, which each family would hold its own copy of.
tells_us.title: Splitting into families duplicates shared content

tells_us.text: Adding one more dependency to each variable multiplies the probability tables by up to 4 times. The number of variables is a much weaker driver of size than how they are connected.
tells_us.title: Structure matters more than scale

tells_us.text: Under the assumptions tested, the probability tables are measured in megabytes and the inference timings in milliseconds. Size is not what distinguishes these options.
tells_us.title: Nothing here is close to a technical limit

tells_us.text: Illustrative running costs are identical across the deployment patterns until volume is high enough to need more than minimum capacity; at 5,000,000 assessments a month they spread to about 2.0x between cheapest and dearest, though the absolute sums remain small. Below that, what distinguishes the patterns is release blast radius, failure scope and version coordination — operational qualities rather than a price.
tells_us.title: Cost separates the patterns only at high volume
